title: Why Do Onions Make You Cry?
summary: Chopping an onion sets off a tiny chemical chain reaction that ends with a gas your eyes hate. Here is how it works, and why the tears are a defence.

beats.text: You slice one onion, and suddenly your eyes are streaming. What did it do to you?

visual.text: Why do onions make you cry?

beats.text: Inside an onion, two things are kept apart in separate compartments. A knife breaks the walls between them.
Once they mix, a quick reaction starts. Which one do you think reaches your eyes?
beats.reveal: A gas! The mix turns into a tiny cloud that floats up from the board.

beats.text: Here is the chain, in three steps.
The gas lands on the wet surface of your eye and makes a mild irritant. Your eye feels a sting.
So your body floods the eye with tears to wash the irritant away. The crying is a cleaning job.
Fewer tears are likely if you chill the onion first, or cut it near a fan, because the reaction slows down and the gas blows away.
The onion does this to protect itself. Nothing wants to bite into something that stings its eyes.

visual.text: BONUS: the onion's gas is a natural defence against animals that might eat it.
